description: Heavy-bodied, blunt-snouted shark common on Jupiter and Palm Beach wrecks and ledges, especially during the winter aggregation. Adults reach 2-3.5 m and often circle close on shark dives.
The shark South Florida divers see most, resting under ledges and in wreck holds by day. Brown with barbels at the nostrils and two dorsal fins set far back; typically 2-3 m.
Gray reef shark with a white belly, seen along the deeper reef lines and wrecks from Jupiter to the Keys. Usually 1.5-2.5 m and often in the mix on baited dives.
Yellowish-brown shark with two near-equal dorsal fins, aggregating on Jupiter wrecks such as the Esso Bonaire in winter. Adults 2.5-3 m, often cruising slowly near the sand.
Largest hammerhead, with a straight-edged head and a tall sickle dorsal fin. Seen in Jupiter and the Keys mostly in winter and spring, often following tarpon and stingrays; can exceed 4 m.
Hammerhead with a notched, scalloped front edge to the head. Occasionally seen in mid-water off Palm Beach and Jupiter, sometimes in small groups; typically 2-3 m.
Large shark with a broad blunt head and fading vertical bars, regularly seen on Jupiter and Palm Beach shark dives. Adults 3-4.5 m, usually curious and slow-moving.
Slim gray shark with black tips on most fins, abundant along the Palm Beach coast during the winter migration. Usually 1.5 m and fast-moving in shallow water.
Slender shark similar to the blacktip but with a more pointed snout, migrating along the Palm Beach coast in huge winter schools. Known for spinning leaps at the surface; around 2 m.
Stocky brownish-gray shark with a very tall first dorsal fin, seen around Jupiter and Palm Beach wrecks. Typically 1.5-2 m.
Sleek oceanic shark with smooth skin and a small first dorsal fin, encountered offshore on blue-water and pelagic dives. Usually 2-2.5 m and inquisitive.
Small hammerhead with a rounded, shovel-shaped head, common in shallow seagrass and sandy areas from Biscayne Bay to the Keys. Usually under 1 m.
Bulky shark with ragged, protruding teeth that hovers motionless near Jupiter wrecks, mostly in summer. Adults 2-3 m and generally docile.
Diamond-shaped gray-brown stingray found buried or feeding on sand flats and patches near reefs throughout South Florida. Discs reach 1.5 m across; watch the tail barb.
Dark ray covered in white spots, with a long whip tail and duck-like snout, often seen gliding along reef lines and over sand. Wingspan up to 3 m, sometimes in small groups.
Huge filter-feeding ray with cephalic fins at the mouth, occasionally seen off Palm Beach and Jupiter. Juveniles appear close to shore in shallow water; adults can span over 5 m.
Small round stingray with a yellow-brown mottled pattern that blends into sand and seagrass near reefs. Disc about 35 cm; easy to miss right beside you.
Small, round-bodied electric ray with brown blotches, found buried in sand near shore and around Blue Heron Bridge. Up to 50 cm; can deliver a mild shock if touched.
Brown ray with a notched, cow-like snout, often seen in large schools migrating along the coast. Wingspan around 1 m.
Bright blue and yellow angelfish with a blue-ringed dark crown spot on the forehead, common on reefs and wrecks. Up to 45 cm.
Black angelfish with yellow-edged scales, usually seen in pairs on reefs and wrecks; juveniles are black with yellow bars and act as cleaners. Up to 40 cm.
Large gray-brown angelfish with a pale mouth and a squared-off tail, often swimming in pairs and approaching divers. Up to 60 cm.
Yellow angelfish with a large black rear body, common on South Florida reefs. Up to 30 cm, often shy and hiding near sponges.
Blue-gray angelfish with yellow-edged fins, similar to the queen angelfish but lacking the crown spot. Common on Palm Beach and Broward reefs; up to 45 cm.
Small silver-gray butterflyfish with a white-ringed black false eyespot near the tail. Very common in pairs on reefs; about 15 cm.
White butterflyfish with yellow fins and a black bar through the eye. Common on shallow reefs and rubble; up to 20 cm.
Pale yellow-tan butterflyfish with a dark band at the rear, found on deeper reefs and ledges. About 15 cm.
White butterflyfish with bold black vertical bands, seen in pairs on reefs and around wrecks. Up to 16 cm.
Common parrotfish whose terminal males are green with a yellow tail spot; females are red and brown. Heard crunching algae off coral; up to 60 cm.
Terminal males are blue-green with orange-edged markings; females are dark with a white stripe. Often grazing in harems on reefs; up to 60 cm.
The largest Atlantic herbivorous fish, with an orange head and green body. Found near shallow reefs and mangroves, especially in the Keys; up to 1.2 m.
Uniformly blue parrotfish; large males develop a prominent squared hump on the snout. Seen on shallow reefs; up to 1.2 m.
Smaller parrotfish with a red-orange band from the mouth; terminal males have a yellow and black spot behind the gill. Very common on reefs; up to 28 cm.
Yellow grunt with diagonal blue-white stripes below the lateral line, forming dense schools under ledges and around wrecks. About 30 cm.
Yellow grunt with straight horizontal blue stripes and a dark tail, very common in schools on reefs. Up to 45 cm.
Silvery-yellow grunt with blue stripes on the head only, abundant on reefs and ledges throughout South Florida. Up to 50 cm.
Yellow-striped silver fish with two black bars through the eye and behind the gill. Common in schools under ledges; up to 40 cm.
Small silvery grunt with yellow horizontal stripes and yellow fins, forming large schools near reefs. About 23 cm.
Grayish snapper with a dark stripe through the eye in some phases, schooling on reefs, wrecks and around Blue Heron Bridge pilings. Up to 60 cm.
Slender snapper with a bright yellow midline stripe and deeply forked yellow tail, often swarming divers on reefs. Up to 75 cm.
Snapper with yellow fins and pale vertical bars, hanging in groups under ledges and around elkhorn coral. Up to 60 cm.
Olive-green to reddish snapper with a small black spot on the upper side and blue lines on the face. Seen on reefs and wrecks; up to 90 cm.
The largest Atlantic snapper, gray with thick lips and large canine teeth. Aggregates on deep wrecks and ledges in summer; can exceed 1.5 m.
Massive mottled brown grouper that gathers on Jupiter and Palm Beach wrecks in August-September to spawn. Protected in Florida; can exceed 2 m and 300 kg.
Large grouper with dark rectangular blotches and a squared tail, seen on reefs and wrecks. Up to 1.5 m.
Reddish-brown grouper with pale blotches and a straight-edged dorsal fin, usually resting on the bottom near ledges. Up to 1 m.
Grouper with five dark vertical bars and a black saddle at the tail base; protected and now uncommon, mostly seen in the Keys. Up to 1 m.
Small grouper covered in red-brown spots, with three to four pale or dark spots along the base of the dorsal fin. Common in holes on reefs; about 30 cm.
Small grouper in red, brown or bicolor phases, with tiny blue spots and two black spots on the lower lip. Common on reefs; about 30 cm.
Pale grouper covered in red spots, with dark-edged dorsal, anal and tail fins. Seen resting on reef and rubble; up to 60 cm.
Large wrasse with a long pig-like snout and long first dorsal spines, rooting in sand near reefs. Males have a dark face band; up to 90 cm.
Abundant small wrasse; most are yellow, while terminal males have a blue head, black and white bands, and a green body. About 15 cm.
Wrasse with a purple-blue upper body and yellow underside; juveniles clean other fish. Common on reefs; up to 40 cm.
Slim greenish wrasse with a dark stripe along the side, very common on shallow reefs, sand and seagrass. About 20 cm.
Large green-blue wrasse with blue lines on the head and a dark spot at the pectoral base. Common on reefs; up to 50 cm.
Terminal males have a yellow head and a dark vertical bar mid-body; juveniles are yellow with a blue stripe. Common on reefs; about 18 cm.
Yellow-backed damselfish with five black vertical bars, often in groups near the surface and wreck structure. Males guard purple egg patches; about 20 cm.
Dark blue-brown damselfish with a yellow tail; juveniles are blue with iridescent blue spots. Common on shallow reefs; about 20 cm.
Brilliant blue planktivore with a black-edged forked tail, hovering in loose schools above the reef. About 13 cm.
Long, flattened filefish with blue scribbles and spots and a broom-like tail, often drifting near sea fans and wrecks. Up to 1 m.
Brown to orange filefish covered in white spots, often seen in pairs around reefs. Up to 45 cm.
Colorful triggerfish with bright blue facial lines and long trailing fin tips, feeding on urchins on reefs and rubble. Up to 60 cm.
Plain gray triggerfish common around wrecks and artificial reefs. Can be territorial when nesting; up to 60 cm.
Black triggerfish with a distinctive pale blue line along the base of the dorsal and anal fins. Seen above deeper reefs and wrecks; about 40 cm.
Box-shaped fish with two horns over the eyes and blue scribble markings, common in seagrass and on shallow reefs. About 40 cm.
Horned box-shaped fish with a hexagonal honeycomb pattern, found on reefs. About 45 cm and able to change shade.
Dark boxfish covered in white spots with a honeycomb pattern on the face, hovering low over sand near reefs. About 30 cm.
Pale boxfish densely covered in black spots, with white lips. Seen on reefs, often under ledges; about 45 cm.
Large spiny puffer with big eyes and small dark spots, often resting under ledges by day. Inflates when threatened; up to 90 cm.
Smaller porcupinefish with long spines and dark blotches, common around Blue Heron Bridge and shallow reefs. About 30 cm.
Tiny pointed-snout puffer, brown above and white below with blue lines, very common on reefs. About 12 cm.
Well-camouflaged ambush predator that lies still on reef and rubble, flashing black-and-white banded pectoral fins when disturbed. Venomous spines; about 30 cm.

Invasive Indo-Pacific fish with red-and-white stripes and long venomous spines, now found on almost every reef and wreck in South Florida. Divers are encouraged to report and remove them; about 35 cm.
Lumpy, sponge-like anglerfish in yellow, red or brown that sits motionless and fishes with a lure. Found at Blue Heron Bridge and on reefs; about 15 cm.
Pale-blue fish with a yellow head that hovers vertically above its burrow in sand and rubble; males brood eggs in their mouths. About 10 cm.
Tiny black goby with an electric-blue stripe that runs cleaning stations on coral heads. About 5 cm.
Dark blenny with red lips and fin margins, perching on shallow coral and rocks. About 12 cm.
Disc-shaped silver fish with dark vertical bars, schooling in mid-water around wrecks and reefs. Up to 90 cm.
Black-and-white striped drum with a very tall first dorsal fin; adults have white spots on the rear fins. Hides under ledges; juveniles are a favorite photo subject. About 25 cm.
Drum with a tall dorsal fin and a single dark band curving from the dorsal fin to the tail, like a jackknife. Shy, under ledges; about 25 cm.
Small striped drum with a tall dorsal fin, hovering in holes and under ledges. About 23 cm.
Red and silver fish with large eyes and a yellow-tipped dorsal fin, sheltering under ledges by day. About 30 cm.
Red squirrelfish with white spots at the dorsal spine tips and a long anal fin spine. Common in reef crevices; about 30 cm.
Red, big-eyed nocturnal fish with a dark bar behind the gill cover, hanging in caves and under ledges. About 20 cm.
Large, deep-bodied gray grunt with a dark patch behind the head, usually seen under ledges and around wrecks. Up to 75 cm.
Long, stick-like fish with a tube mouth that hangs head-down among sea rods or shadows other fish to ambush prey. Up to 90 cm.
Flatfish covered in blue rings and spots that changes color to match the sand, often seen near reefs and at Blue Heron Bridge. Up to 45 cm.
Lizardfish that rests propped on its fins on sand or reef, then darts up to grab prey. About 30 cm.
Gray-brown surgeonfish with a crescent tail, grazing in schools over reefs. About 35 cm.
Deep-bodied surgeonfish, bright yellow as juveniles and deep blue as adults, often in large grazing schools on reefs. About 35 cm.
Surgeonfish with about 10 thin vertical bars on its body, schooling with other tangs. About 35 cm.
Tiny fish with a purple front half and yellow rear, often swimming upside down under ledges. About 8 cm; more common in the Keys.
Small sea bass with tan and brown vertical bars and blue lines on the face, hovering near the reef. About 15 cm.
Silver-gray fish with black vertical bars and human-like teeth, common around bridge pilings, jetties and inlets. Up to 75 cm.
Seahorse in varied colors with fine white lines, found holding onto seagrass, sponges and debris at Blue Heron Bridge. About 15 cm.
Flattened bottom fish that walks on its pectoral fins over sand and rubble, with a red-lipped face. A favorite find at Blue Heron Bridge; about 30 cm.
Bottom fish that walks over sand and spreads large blue-edged fan-like pectoral fins when startled. Seen at Blue Heron Bridge; about 45 cm.
Gray, oval-bodied fish with faint yellow lines, schooling near the surface over reefs and wrecks. Up to 75 cm.
Red fish with very large eyes and a protruding lower jaw, seen near ledges and on deeper reefs. About 40 cm.
Long silver predator with dark blotches and a jutting jaw full of teeth, hovering near divers over reefs and wrecks. Up to 1.8 m; curious but rarely a threat.
Huge silver fish with large mirror-like scales and an upturned mouth, schooling around Palm Beach and Jupiter wrecks and in the Keys. Up to 2.5 m.
Deep-bodied silver jack with a forked dark tail, aggregating on Jupiter and Palm Beach wrecks to spawn in spring and summer. Up to 1.2 m.
Long, dark brown fish with a flat head and a pale stripe along the side, often seen following sharks, rays or divers near wrecks. Up to 2 m.
Large silver jack with a dark diagonal band through the eye, schooling around deep wrecks and circling divers. Up to 1.8 m.
Silvery, deep-bodied jack with a steep forehead, cruising around deep wrecks and reef ledges. Juveniles have long trailing filaments; adults reach 1.3 m.
Long, silver mackerel with a sharply dipping lateral line, passing fast along reefs and wrecks. Up to 1.7 m.
Brilliant green and gold fish with a long dorsal fin, found offshore near floating sargassum. Bull males have a steep blunt head; up to 1.5 m.
Billfish with a huge sail-like dorsal fin, occasionally seen on blue-water dives off Palm Beach and Jupiter in winter. Up to 3 m including the bill.
Bluish-silver jack with a blunt head and a black spot on the gill cover, schooling fast over reefs and inlets. Up to 1 m.
Silver jack with a large eye and yellow-tinged tail, forming large swirling schools around wrecks and reefs. Up to 1 m.
Silvery jack with a dark stripe running along the back into the lower tail lobe, often following feeding rays and fish. About 40 cm.
Slender fish with a sucking disk on its head that rides on sharks, rays and turtles and sometimes tries to attach to divers. Up to 1 m.
The largest local moray, uniformly green, poking its head out of reef and wreck holes. Up to 2.5 m.
Pale moray densely covered in dark spots, very common in reef crevices. Up to 1.2 m.
Small dark-brown moray with yellow spots and a yellow tail tip, hiding in reef holes. About 60 cm.
Snake eel with pale spots that hunts in the open over reef, sand and seagrass during the day. Up to 1 m.
Thin eels that live in colonies on sandy bottoms, rising from their burrows and retreating when divers approach. About 50 cm.
Reddish-brown turtle with a large head, frequently seen resting under ledges and on wrecks off Palm Beach and Jupiter. Shell up to about 1 m; nests on local beaches in summer.
Turtle with a small rounded head and smooth shell, often grazing seagrass and algae on shallow reefs. Shell up to about 1.2 m.
Smaller turtle with a hawk-like beak and overlapping shell plates, often feeding on sponges on the reef. Shell up to about 90 cm; critically endangered.
The smallest local sea turtle, gray-green with a nearly round shell. Rarely seen by divers; shell about 65 cm.
Huge turtle with a ridged, leathery black shell instead of plates, occasionally seen offshore and nesting on Palm Beach County beaches. Can exceed 2 m.
Gray dolphin with a short stubby beak, common in coastal waters, inlets and over reefs. About 2.5-3 m; sometimes passes divers on safety stops.
Dolphin that becomes heavily spotted with age, seen offshore and on the boat ride out. About 2 m.
Large, slow, gray herbivore with a paddle tail, seen in canals, inlets and around Blue Heron Bridge, especially in winter. Up to 4 m; protected - do not touch or harass.
Branching coral with antler-like brown branches, now mostly found in restoration nurseries and outplant sites from Broward to the Keys. Critically endangered.
Branching coral with thick, flattened, moose-antler branches on shallow reef crests in the Keys. Critically endangered and the focus of restoration work.
Hemispherical brain coral with a deep groove running along the top of each ridge. Common on Keys reefs.
Rounded brain coral with even, symmetrical valleys and ridges, common on shallow reefs. Heavily affected by stony coral tissue loss disease.
Large brain coral with wide, deep valleys, forming big domes on reefs. Can exceed 2 m across.
Boulder or plate coral with large, round polyps, one of the most common reef-building corals on Palm Beach and Broward reefs. Often green or brown and fluorescent at night.
Major Caribbean reef builder forming lumpy columns and lobes with small polyps. Found mainly in the Keys; threatened.
Yellow-green to brown lumpy encrusting coral, very common on shallow reefs throughout South Florida.
Branching coral with short, thick, finger-like branches in tan or gray, often forming thickets on shallow reefs.
Thin, plate-like coral with leafy ridges, encrusting or forming small plates on reefs.
Non-native, non-reef-building coral with bright orange polyps that covers wreck surfaces. Polyps extend at night; invasive in Florida.
Purple or yellow lattice-like fan that grows at right angles to the current on shallow reefs. Up to 1.5 m tall.
Soft coral with dark branching rods and tan polyps, common on shallow reefs alongside other gorgonians.
Soft coral forming upright purple-gray fingers or encrusting mats, with fuzzy brown polyps when extended.
Mustard-yellow hydrozoan (not a true coral) that encrusts surfaces and grows branching tips, often over sea fans and wrecks. Stings bare skin on contact.
Yellow-brown hydrozoan forming upright flat blades with white tips on shallow reefs. Stings on contact.
Huge reddish-brown barrel-shaped sponge with a rough exterior, common on deeper reefs. Can exceed 2 m across and live for centuries.
Bright yellow sponge growing in clusters of tubes, common on reefs and often photographed.
Pinkish-purple vase-shaped sponge that glows blue in some light, with a ridged surface. Found on reefs; about 30 cm tall.
Large orange sponge forming ear-like or fan-shaped plates on reefs and wall edges.
Red-orange sponge that bores into and slowly overgrows living corals, visible as red patches with large openings on coral heads.
Clawless lobster with long spiny antennae, peeking out from under ledges and in wreck holes. Up to 45 cm; harvested during the summer mini-season.
Flattened lobster with plate-like antennae instead of spiny ones, hiding in crevices by day. About 30 cm.
Red-and-white banded cleaner shrimp with long white antennae, usually in pairs under ledges. About 6 cm.
Spider-like crab with a triangular pointed head and very long thin legs, often among anemones and sponges. About 6 cm body.
Large spiny reddish crab that hides in reef crevices by day and forages at night. Body up to 18 cm.
Transparent shrimp with white saddles and purple spots, living on anemones such as the giant Caribbean anemone. About 2.5 cm.
Transparent shrimp with purple and white markings that lives on corkscrew anemones and waves to attract fish to clean. About 2.5 cm.
Large red hermit crab living in queen conch and horse conch shells, seen on sand and seagrass at night and at Blue Heron Bridge.
Heavy crab with large black-tipped claws, hiding in rocky holes and under ledges near shore.
Small, translucent shrimp with red stripes, living in groups in reef crevices and sponges. About 5 cm.
Iridescent blue-green octopus that hunts over reefs and seagrass at night. Arm span up to 60 cm.
Brown, highly variable octopus found in reef holes and wreck debris, often given away by a midden of shells at its den. Arm span up to 1 m.
Squid with fins running the length of its mantle, hovering in small lines over shallow reefs and changing color. About 20 cm.
Tiny octopus that lives in empty shells and bottles, often found at Blue Heron Bridge on night dives. About 15 cm across.
Green sacoglossan slug with ruffled, lettuce-like parapodia, found on shallow reefs and rubble. Up to 5 cm.
Small snail with a spotted orange mantle covering its shell, feeding on sea fans and sea rods. About 3 cm; do not collect.
Large sea snail with a flaring pink-lipped shell, found on sand and seagrass, mostly in the Keys. Harvest is prohibited in Florida; up to 30 cm.
Large sea slug with dark rings on a green-brown body, releasing purple ink when disturbed. Common at Blue Heron Bridge; up to 20 cm.
Clam with a red mantle and fringe of red or white tentacles, tucked into reef crevices. About 7 cm.
One of the largest sea snails in the world, with an orange body and spindle-shaped shell, found in seagrass and sand. Florida's state shell; up to 60 cm.
Black urchin with very long, sharp spines that hides in reef crevices by day. A key algae grazer whose 1983 and 2022 die-offs hurt Florida reefs.
Thick, five-armed sea star in orange to brown with a raised net pattern, on sand and seagrass. Up to 50 cm.
Short-spined urchin in green, pink or white, often covering itself with shells and seagrass. About 10 cm.
Large dark urchin with short white spines, found in seagrass and on shallow reefs. About 15 cm.
Reddish-brown to black urchin that bores into rock in shallow, wave-exposed areas. About 15 cm.
Brittle star that sits coiled on gorgonians by day and unfurls its finely branching arms to filter plankton at night.
Large sea cucumber with dark knobby spots, sifting through sand near reefs and in seagrass. Up to 45 cm.
Translucent saucer-shaped jelly with four horseshoe-shaped gonads visible in the bell. Blooms near shore; mild sting.
Colonial siphonophore (not a true jellyfish) with a blue gas float and long trailing tentacles, blown ashore in winter. Painful sting, even from washed-up specimens.
Jellyfish that lies bell-down on the bottom in shallow lagoons and mangroves, especially in the Keys. Mild sting; about 20 cm.
Firm, dome-shaped jelly with a brown-edged bell, often seen in coastal waters in large numbers. About 20 cm; weak sting.
Tube worm with colorful spiral plumes embedded in coral heads that retracts instantly when approached. Plumes about 3 cm.
Bristle worm with white tufts of stinging bristles along the sides, crawling over reefs and feeding on corals. Up to 30 cm; do not touch.
Large anemone with thick tentacles, often pink- or purple-tipped, hosting cleaner shrimps. Up to 30 cm across.
Anemone with translucent tentacles marked with spiral white rings, living in crevices and hosting Pederson cleaner shrimp.
Small fan worms that grow in clusters with brown or white feather-like crowns, common on reefs and wrecks.
Small, fast wrasse on shallow South Florida reefs and rubble. Terminal-phase males are green with a dark lateral spot and a yellow-orange belly; juveniles and females are paler with a dark stripe.
Silvery-white goatfish with a bright yellow stripe from eye to tail and a yellow tail, often in loose schools over sand next to the reef. Probes the sand with its two chin barbels.

Goatfish with three dark blotches along its side that can flush reddish; usually alone or in pairs, rooting through sand and rubble with its chin barbels while other fish follow to grab what it stirs up.

Small, flattened batfish that 'walks' over sand and rubble on its stiff pectoral and pelvic fins. Rough, warty skin and a short snout with a tiny lure; a lucky find on South Florida sand flats near reefs.
